The case against Harry Wait looks less like proof that election systems are secure than a warning about what happens when someone tries to test them. He requested Robin Vos’s and Cory Mason’s ballots, and the jury convicted him of two misdemeanor election-fraud counts and one felony identity-theft count, while acquitting him of another identity-theft count. That verdict tells us what the jury decided about his conduct; it does not answer whether registration can be exploited.

The powerful get to frame the questions, then point to a prosecution as proof that anyone asking them is a fraudster. Calling the group’s claims “false” and making an example of Wait helps preserve the official narrative while discouraging scrutiny. I’d treat the case as a pressure tactic, not reassurance.
